newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czechs snub Senate polls amid confusion and sleaze.
newsitem.headline: Czechs snub Senate polls amid confusion and sleaze.

text.p: Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus has hailed his party's strong showing in Senate elections as a public yearning for economic reform with stability. But the truth is no party really won and democracy was the big loser.

The dismal turnout at the weekend tells a different story from Klaus: Czechs are at best confused about what the Senate will do and at worst in despair about the sleaze and petty-mindedness which surrounds Czech politics.
Figures from the first round of Senate polls on Friday and Saturday look good for Klaus, who has been under pressure since his coalition government lost its lower house majority in June.
His centre-right Civic Democratic Party (ODS) won 36.5 percent of the vote, well up from 29.6 percent in June.
Klaus, who has led Czech economic reform since the 1989 fall of communism, warned supporters that almost all ODS candidates faced a second round run-off on November 22 and 23.
But he neverthless gloated as the results came in on Saturday evening. "I think that the results known so far are very good. It would be false modesty not to say so," he said.

"I would like to thank our voters who have realised that our country is threatened by instability and a backward move which, I think, we should not allow," he said on the eve of the seventh anniversary of the 1989 overthrow of communism.
But turnout at just 34 percent compared with 76 percent in the lower house polls puts the ODS performance into context.
ODS, well organised and well funded by big business, was simply better at getting its supporters out than its rivals.

Klaus expressed indifference to the turnout. "I'm saying here publicly that my aim is not the maximum number of votes, my aim is the maximum number of votes for the ODS," he said on a television debate, challenging his rivals to admit the same.
Speculation is growing over whether Klaus might seek early lower house elections to try to regain his majority. But he may be ill-advised to draw any firm conclusions.
"He doesn't know how the 70 percent who stayed at home would vote," said Jiri Pehe, director of research at the Open Media Research Insitute (OMRI).
The question is why did those 70 percent of voters, or more precisely 66 percent, stay at home?

Undoubtedly voters were confused. The Senate is new and few people except President Vaclav Havel, who led the nation back to democracy in 1989, seemed enthusiastic about it. Few Czechs understand its powers and also the voting system was new.
But the low turnout may indicate a deeper malaise. "It's not a good result for anyone. It is caused by disgust with politics as practised in this country," said Pehe.
Czech politics has been rocked for years by a series of scandals. Many involved fraud allegations and yet hardly anyone significant has ever been caught.

The months leading to the Senate elections were marked by a series of banking collapses involving murky stock dealings, and allegations from the deputy prime minister and Christian Democrat leader Josef Lux that the state intelligence agency had spied on him and then covered up the operation.
The agency's director Stanislav Devaty, a Klaus protege, was forced to resign and an investigation announced. But past experience shows Czechs are unlikely ever to hear the truth.
"What people are looking for is some kind of decency and transparency. Average people are fed up with the notion of widespread corruption," said Pehe.
It is not only average people. In his New Year's message, Havel expressed his concern about "the alarming extent of corruption, which unfortunately is not proved in most cases".
"People feel they cannot achieve anything by voting," said Pehe. "It is a rather unhappy situation for the democratic process in this country."
